shaper_tab.help_text:
Input Shaper is a technology that helps reduce vibrations in a 3D printer during printing.

Vibrations can cause defects on the model, such as 'ghosting'. Input Shaper analyzes the printer's movements and adjusts them to minimize these vibrations.

How it works?
1. Load accelerometer data.
2. The program selects the best 'shaper'.
3. Copy the settings.

Result: smoother printing and fewer defects!

guide.title: How do I get the bed mesh? (beginners)
guide.intro: A bed mesh is a measurement of bed height at many points. The printer makes it during auto-leveling and saves it in printer.cfg. That file is what you load here.
guide.measure_title: Measure the bed on the printer
guide.measure_1: Heat the bed to your usual printing temperature (e.g. 60 °C for PLA) — a cold and a hot bed differ.
guide.measure_2: Run bed auto-leveling (calibration/leveling) on the printer and wait for it to finish. The result is saved to the config.
guide.export_title: Export printer.cfg to a USB stick

guide.load_text: Drag printer.cfg into the window or press the button. The file never leaves your computer — everything runs in the browser.

spectrogram.no_raw: A spectrogram needs the raw accelerometer CSV (calibration_data_*.csv with time, accel_x, accel_y, accel_z). This file holds an already computed spectrum, so the time axis is gone.
spectrogram.guide_1: Horizontal is frequency, vertical is test progress from start (0%) to end (100%). Brighter means stronger vibration.
spectrogram.guide_2: During the test Klipper shakes the toolhead at a steadily rising frequency — that shows up as a slanted bright line. That is normal.
spectrogram.guide_3: A bright vertical band is the axis resonance: the printer "rings" at that frequency. That is what the shaper cancels; the green dotted line is the recommended frequency and should sit inside the band.
spectrogram.guide_4: A narrow, sharp band is good. A wide, smeared band means a loose belt, carriage play or a flexible frame.
spectrogram.guide_5: Two bands close together (e.g. 45 and 55 Hz) on CoreXY usually mean the two belts have different tension. Even them out and re-test.
spectrogram.guide_6: Bright spots only at certain moments, or bands above 100 Hz through the whole test, mean something rattles: a fan, a cable, a loose accelerometer or screw.
spectrogram.guide_7: Before re-testing, turn off the fans and check the sensor mount, or their noise ends up in the graph.

stencil.title: Tape stencil — print it once
stencil.step_1: Print the stencil on the PEI sheet: PLA, 0.2 mm layers, no supports. The slicer centres it on the bed by itself.
stencil.step_2: Peel the stencil off the PEI, then remove the PEI itself.
stencil.step_3: Lay the stencil on the magnetic base with letters A–E towards you (front edge), centred.
stencil.step_4: Stick tape in the windows listed above: as many pieces stacked as layers. One piece is about a window, ~39×39 mm.
stencil.step_5: Remove the stencil, put the PEI back and take a new mesh.
stencil.hint: Letters A–E on the stencil mark the front edge, numbers 1–5 the left edge. A1 is the front-left corner, as in the diagram above.
